questions.explanation: A proposition is a declarative statement with a definite truth value. '7 is prime' is true.

questions.prompt: If p is true and q is false, what is the value of p AND q?
questions.explanation: A conjunction is true only when both of its parts are true.

questions.prompt: In inclusive logic, what is the value of p OR q when both p and q are true?
choices: It depends on which is written first.
questions.explanation: Inclusive OR is true when at least one part is true, including when both are true.

questions.prompt: When is the implication p implies q false?
choices: When p and q are both true
When p is false and q is true
When p is true and q is false
When p and q are both false
questions.explanation: An implication is false only when its condition p is true but its conclusion q is false.

questions.prompt: When is p if and only if q true?
choices: When p and q have the same truth value
When p and q have different truth values
questions.explanation: A biconditional is true when both sides agree: both true or both false.

questions.prompt: How many rows are needed for a truth table with three propositions?
questions.explanation: Each of the three propositions has two possible truth values, so there are 2^3 = 8 assignments.

questions.prompt: If p is false and q is false, what is the value of p implies q?
questions.explanation: An implication is false only for true p and false q. With p false, it is true.

questions.prompt: Which expression is logically equivalent to p implies q?
questions.explanation: Both p implies q and NOT p OR q are false only when p is true and q is false.

questions.prompt: What is equivalent to NOT (p AND q)?
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law changes the conjunction to OR and negates each proposition.

questions.prompt: If p implies q is true, what can you conclude about q implies p?
choices: It has the same truth value as p.
The original implication does not determine it.
questions.explanation: An implication does not guarantee its converse. For example, being a rectangle does not guarantee being a square.

questions.prompt: Over the integers, what is a witness showing that there exists an x such that x = 2?
questions.explanation: An existential claim is established by one value in its domain that satisfies the predicate; x = 2 does.

questions.prompt: What is enough to show that a statement of the form 'for every x, P(x)' is false?
choices: One counterexample where P(x) is false
One example where P(x) is true
Two examples where P(x) is true
questions.explanation: A universal statement is false as soon as one domain member fails to satisfy P.

questions.prompt: Which statement is equivalent to NOT (for every x, P(x))?
choices: There exists an x such that NOT P(x)
There exists an x such that P(x)
questions.explanation: Negating a universal quantifier produces an existential quantifier and negates its predicate.

questions.prompt: Which statement is equivalent to NOT (there exists an x such that P(x))?
choices: There exists an x such that NOT P(x)
NOT P(x) for one chosen x
questions.explanation: If no domain member satisfies P, then every domain member satisfies NOT P.

questions.prompt: Over the natural numbers, how can you show that for every n there exists an m greater than n?
choices: Choose one fixed m for every n
questions.explanation: For each natural number n, choosing m = n + 1 gives a natural number greater than n.
